content: The Guideline Steering Group developed specific PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparator, and Outcome) questions to guide systematic reviews that would support the creation of the guidelines. Two key PICO questions were identified as relevant to these guidelines: 1. Do packaged interventions, which involve the delivery of two or more interventions together, improve outcomes in individuals with advanced HIV disease compared to standard care? Advanced HIV disease is defined by the WHO as a CD4 count of less than 200 cells/mm³ and/or WHO stage 3 or 4 disease. 2. Does the rapid initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART), including same-day initiation, result in better outcomes for individuals newly diagnosed with HIV? A list of potential outcomes of interest for each question was distributed to all members of the Guideline Development Group. Members rated the importance of each outcome on a scale from 1 (not important) to 9 (critical). The median score for each outcome was used to inform decision-making. Systematic review teams created protocols and conducted reviews in accordance with PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) guidelines. These reviews are available in the Web Annex accompanying the guidelines. To explore values and preferences, an online survey was conducted among people living with HIV. The survey assessed the acceptability of packaged interventions for advanced HIV disease and the acceptability of rapid or same-day ART initiation. The survey was disseminated through networks of civil society organizations and representative organizations of people living with HIV. Additionally, a qualitative literature review was conducted to further support the evidence for rapid or same-day ART initiation. Results from a community-led global consultation on this topic were also reviewed. To assess the feasibility and acceptability of both packaged interventions for advanced HIV disease and rapid or same-day ART initiation, online surveys were conducted among healthcare workers and HIV program managers. Healthcare workers were contacted through existing networks of healthcare organizations, while program managers were reached via WHO regional advisers, who distributed the surveys to country program managers in their respective regions. The systematic review for packaged interventions identified evidence regarding the costs of these interventions. Unit costs and cost-effectiveness, where available, were evaluated as part of the review. The quality of evidence and the strength of recommendations were assessed using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) methodology. The GRADE approach, adopted by WHO, defines the quality of evidence as the degree of confidence that the reported estimates of effect (whether beneficial or harmful) are close to the actual effects. The strength of a recommendation reflects the confidence of the Guideline Development Group that the desirable effects of the recommendation outweigh the undesirable effects. Desirable effects may include improved health outcomes (e.g., reduced morbidity and mortality), reduced burden on individuals and health services, and potential cost savings. Undesirable effects may include harm to individuals, families, communities, or health services, as well as additional burdens such as resource use and cost implications. Clinical outcomes, such as drug resistance and toxicity, were also considered. A strong recommendation indicates high confidence that the desirable effects of adherence to the recommendation clearly outweigh the undesirable effects. A conditional recommendation suggests that the quality of evidence may be low, apply only to specific groups or settings, or that the desirable effects probably outweigh the undesirable effects, but the trade-offs are less certain. The quality of evidence, values and preferences of end-users, feasibility, resource implications, and potential benefits and harms all contributed to determining the strength of a recommendation. The Guideline Development Group convened for three days in Geneva, Switzerland, from March 22 to 24, 2017. During this meeting, systematic reviews and supporting evidence, including values and preferences, acceptability, feasibility, and cost, were presented. Evidence-to-decision-making tables were prepared following the GRADE process and presented to the group. Discussions were facilitated by a methodologist, and decisions were made by unanimous consensus. Voting was not required, but the group had agreed beforehand that a 60% majority would be needed for a decision if voting became necessary. A draft of the guidelines was circulated for peer review to members of the Guideline Development Group and the External Review Group. The Guideline Steering Group reviewed the comments and incorporated them into the final document, taking into account any conflicts of interest declared by members of the External Review Group. All external contributors to the guideline development process completed a WHO declaration of interests form. In line with WHO’s policy on declarations of interest for experts, a brief biography of each Guideline Development Group member was published on the WHO HIV website for 14 days, along with a description of the meeting’s objectives. No public comments or objections were received regarding the group members. The responsible technical officer reviewed all declarations of interest submitted by the Guideline Development Group members and conducted a complementary web search. A management plan was agreed upon for each declared conflict of interest. All declared interests and management strategies were discussed with the chairs and methodologist. Conflicts of interest were disclosed at the start of the Guideline Development Group meeting, and participation was closely monitored by the Guideline Steering Group and the GRADE methodologist. The majority of the Guideline Development Group members did not declare significant conflicts of interest for this meeting. Efforts were made to minimize conflicts of interest in the group’s representation. However, the Guideline Steering Group acknowledged the challenges of limiting the participation of key experts, as pharmaceutical companies play a significant role in HIV research and antiretroviral drug trials, and many experts are involved as investigators in relevant trials. The Guideline Steering Group assessed all completed declarations of interest forms for other external contributors to the guidelines. Individual participation was reviewed in light of the declared interests.
